title: Design a URL shortener
prompt: Design a service that turns long URLs into short links and redirects visitors who open them.
clarify: How many new links per month and what is the read-to-write ratio?
Do links expire, and can users choose custom aliases?
Do we need click analytics, or only redirects?
strongAnswer: States scale first: for example 100 million links a month is about 40 writes per second and roughly 400 reads per second.
Generates unique short ids without collisions: a counter encoded in base 62, or random ids with a uniqueness check, and explains the trade-off.
Chooses a key-value or simple relational store keyed by short id, because access is by key only.
Puts a cache in front for reads, since links rarely change, and says what hit ratio it aims for.
Discusses redirect status codes: 301 is cacheable by browsers, 302 lets you count every click.
Covers expiry, abuse (malicious links) and what happens if the id generator fails.
pitfalls: Hashing the URL and ignoring collisions.
A single counter that is a single point of failure.
Sharding or microservices before any number justifies them.

title: Design a distributed rate limiter
prompt: Design a rate limiting service that many API servers call to decide whether to accept or reject each request.
clarify: What are we limiting by: user, API key, IP or endpoint?
Hard limit or tolerate small overshoot?
If the limiter is unavailable, should requests be allowed (fail open) or blocked?
strongAnswer: Compares algorithms: fixed window, sliding window log, sliding window counter and token bucket, and picks one with a reason (token bucket allows bursts).
Keeps counters in a fast shared store such as Redis, with atomic updates (a script or atomic increment) to avoid race conditions between servers.
Describes the key design, for example limit:{apiKey}:{window}, and expiry so counters clean themselves up.
Returns standard responses: HTTP 429 with Retry-After and remaining-limit headers.
Discusses latency of the extra hop, local caching or approximate counting, and the fail-open versus fail-closed decision.
Handles hot keys, multiple regions and how limits are configured and changed.
pitfalls: Read-then-write counters that race across servers.
Ignoring the burst-at-the-boundary problem of fixed windows.
No plan for the limiter itself failing.

title: Design a chat application
prompt: Design a messaging service that supports one-to-one and group chat with delivery to online and offline users.
clarify: How many users and messages per second, and what is the maximum group size?
Do we need message history, read receipts, presence and media?
Is end-to-end encryption in scope?
strongAnswer: Uses persistent connections (WebSocket) through gateway servers for real-time delivery, with a registry of which gateway holds which user.
Gives every message a per-conversation sequence number so ordering is well defined, and explains why a global ordering is unnecessary.
Stores messages in a write-optimised store partitioned by conversation, with a separate path for media in object storage.
Handles offline users with a durable inbox and push notifications, and acknowledges delivery and read states.
Covers group fan-out and how to limit its cost for large groups.
Discusses presence at scale (heartbeats with coarse updates) and reconnection with message catch-up.
pitfalls: Polling instead of a push channel.
Assuming messages arrive once and in order without acknowledgements.
Storing media inside the message database.

title: Design a notification system
prompt: Design a system that sends push, email and SMS notifications triggered by events from many services.
clarify: Which channels and what volume per day, including peaks?
Are some notifications urgent and others batchable?
Do users control preferences and quiet hours?
strongAnswer: Accepts events through an API or queue and decouples producers from delivery with durable queues per channel.
Applies user preferences, templates and localisation in a processing stage before sending.
Uses third-party providers behind adapters, with retries and exponential backoff, and a dead-letter queue for permanent failures.
Prevents duplicates with an idempotency key per notification, since delivery is at-least-once.
Rate limits per user and per provider, and prioritises urgent messages over bulk ones.
Tracks delivery status and exposes metrics for failures and latency.
pitfalls: Sending synchronously from the request path.
No duplicate protection when retrying.
One shared queue where bulk traffic delays urgent messages.

title: Design a social news feed
prompt: Design the home feed for a social network where users see recent posts from the people they follow.
clarify: How many users, how many follow whom, and how often do people post and read?
Is the feed chronological or ranked?
How fresh must the feed be?
strongAnswer: Contrasts fan-out on write (precompute each follower's feed) with fan-out on read (assemble when requested) and the cost of each.
Proposes a hybrid: fan-out on write for most users, fan-out on read for accounts with huge follower counts.
Stores timelines as capped lists in a cache or fast store, with posts stored once and referenced by id.
Uses cursor-based pagination so the feed stays stable as new posts arrive.
Separates ranking from retrieval and explains where ranking would plug in.
Handles deleted posts, new follows and cold users with an empty cached feed.
pitfalls: Ignoring the celebrity problem.
Offset pagination on a feed that changes.
Storing full post bodies in every follower's timeline.

title: Design search autocomplete
prompt: Design a typeahead service that suggests completions as the user types a search query.
clarify: What latency budget do we have per keystroke?
How are suggestions ranked and how fresh must they be?
Is personalisation in scope?
strongAnswer: Notes the budget is tens of milliseconds, so lookups must come from memory with results precomputed.
Uses a prefix structure such as a trie, or a key-value map from prefix to its top-k suggestions, rather than scanning queries.
Builds suggestion data offline from query logs and refreshes it periodically; real-time updates are a separate, smaller path.
Caches common prefixes at the edge and in the service, and debounces requests on the client.
Shards by prefix with awareness of skew (very common prefixes).
Filters unsafe or low-quality suggestions.
pitfalls: Querying a database with LIKE on every keystroke.
Rebuilding the structure synchronously on every new query.
Ignoring client-side debouncing and caching.

title: Design a web crawler
prompt: Design a crawler that discovers and downloads billions of web pages for a search index.
clarify: How many pages and how fresh must the index be?
Which content types matter, and must we respect robots.txt?
Do we only crawl, or also parse and extract links?
strongAnswer: Describes the loop: a URL frontier, fetchers, a parser that extracts links, and deduplication before re-queuing.
Builds the frontier with priorities and per-host politeness (rate limit and delay per domain) so sites are not overloaded.
Deduplicates URLs and page content using normalisation and hashing, with a Bloom filter or similar to save memory.
Respects robots.txt, caches DNS lookups and handles timeouts, redirects and crawler traps.
Distributes work by hashing hosts to workers so one host is handled by one worker.
Stores raw pages in object storage and metadata in a database, with re-crawl scheduling by change frequency.
pitfalls: A single queue with no politeness controls.
Treating the URL string as the identity without normalisation.
No protection against infinite link spaces.
